```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Two-level latent class analysis estimates latent classes of categorical
responses at the level of single observations and, above them, latent group
classes that differ in how probable each class is for their observations. In
the output the observation-level classes are called profiles. Each profile is
described by the probability of every answer to every item; the group classes
differ only in how often their observations fall in each profile.

The question here is whether the leisure activities that university students
report in daily life form a small number of recurring patterns, and whether
students differ in how often they are in each pattern.

## Data

`student_esm` holds experience-sampling data from a study of university
students (Neubauer & Schmiedek, 2024). The students answered six prompts a day
for fourteen days. At each prompt when they had not studied since the previous
one, they reported which of eight leisure activities they had done. The
dataset holds these prompts for 100 students: 2,582 prompts, between 15 and 51
per student. Prompts are the observations and students the groups, so a
student contributes many rows.

The eight activities are yes/no items, and they are named once so that each
model can refer to them.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
```

`summary()` counts the answers to each activity item and summarizes the other
variables.

```{r counts}
summary(student_esm)
```

Social media is the most frequent activity, reported at 745 of the 2,582
prompts, followed by TV or video games at 549. A part-time job is the rarest,
at 103 prompts. Every item is answered "no" at most prompts, so a profile is
described by how much more often than average its prompts say "yes".

## The model

For prompt $t$ of student $i$, let $C_{it}$ be the profile and $G_i$ the
student's class. The model estimates three sets of probabilities:

- the response probabilities $\theta_{kjc}=P(Y_{itj}=c\mid C_{it}=k)$ of each
  answer $c$ to item $j$ in profile $k$, the same in every student class;
- the profile probabilities $\pi_{k\mid m}=P(C_{it}=k\mid G_i=m)$ of each
  student class $m$, which sum to one across profiles;
- the class probabilities $\omega_m=P(G_i=m)$.

The items are assumed independent given the profile, the prompts of a student
independent given the student's class, and the students independent of one
another. The likelihood can have several local maxima, so each model is
started from several random values. A rare answer can drive a response
probability to its lower bound, and too many profiles or classes for the data
show up as starts that fail to reach the same maximum.


## How many profiles and classes

`enumerate_classes()` fits every combination of two to four profiles and one
to three student classes, each from twenty random starts with a tight
convergence tolerance, and reports the information criteria and the
diagnostics of each fit. It does not choose a model.

```{r enumerate}
candidates <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, vars = activities,
                                categorical = activities, id = "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                                n_starts = 20, tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
as.data.frame(candidates)
get_results(candidates, "best")
```

```{r enumerate-values, include = FALSE}
grid <- as.data.frame(candidates)
bic_choice <- subset(grid, bic_groups == min(bic_groups))
icl_choice <- subset(grid, icl_individual == min(icl_individual))
awe_choice <- subset(grid, awe_individual == min(awe_individual))
clc_choice <- subset(grid, clc_individual == min(clc_individual))
single_start <- with(subset(grid, n_best_replicated == 1), candidate)
# The text below names these choices; stop if the results ever change.
stopifnot(with(bic_choice, candidate) == "classes4_groups3",
          with(icl_choice, candidate) == "classes3_groups2",
          with(awe_choice, candidate) == "classes3_groups2",
          with(clc_choice, candidate) == "classes3_groups2",
          identical(single_start, c("classes3_groups3", "classes4_groups3")))
```

The criteria disagree, and the diagnostics explain why. BIC with the number of
students keeps falling up to the largest model in the grid, four profiles and
three classes. That model and the one with three profiles and three classes
reach their best solution from a single start (`n_best_replicated`), so their
low BIC rests on solutions that the starts do not replicate. The criteria that
also penalize classification uncertainty (ICL, AWE and CLC counted over
prompts) choose three profiles and two classes, a model whose best solution
recurs in `r with(icl_choice, n_best_replicated)` of the twenty starts.

The number of starts is part of the analysis on these data. With five starts
and the default tolerance, the three-profile, two-class model stops at a lower
maximum of the likelihood, and the same criteria then choose two profiles and
two classes.

The ICL plot shows the choice across the grid.

```{r icl-plot}
plot_enumeration(candidates, what = "icl_individual")
```

The plot marks the minimum at three profiles and two classes, and the analysis
continues with that model.

## The chosen model

`multilca()` fits it, treating every item as categorical, with twenty random
starts and a tight convergence tolerance, which the standard errors below need.

```{r fit}
lca <- multilca(student_esm, vars = activities, id = "student",
                n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 20,
                tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
get_results(lca, "model")
```

```{r fit-values, include = FALSE}
fit_summary <- get_results(lca, "model")
```

The fit converges, and `r with(fit_summary, n_best_replicated)` of the twenty
starts reach the best log likelihood of
`r with(fit_summary, round(log_likelihood))`.

## Three activity profiles

The `"responses"` table gives the probability of each answer in each profile,
with a "no" and a "yes" row for every item. The "yes" rows carry the
information, since the two probabilities of an item sum to one.

```{r responses}
get_results(lca, "responses")
```

```{r profile-values, include = FALSE}
yes <- subset(get_results(lca, "responses"), category == "yes")
answer <- function(k, item) {
  with(subset(yes, profile == k & indicator == item), sprintf("%.3f", probability))
}
job_profile <- with(subset(yes, indicator == "part_time_job" & probability > 0.9),
                    profile)
media_profile <- with(subset(yes, indicator == "on_social_media" & probability > 0.5),
                      profile)
low_profile <- with(yes, setdiff(unique(profile), c(job_profile, media_profile)))
job_others <- with(subset(yes, profile == job_profile & indicator != "part_time_job"),
                   max(probability))
# The text below names the profiles by these patterns; stop if they change.
stopifnot(length(job_profile) == 1L, length(media_profile) == 1L,
          length(low_profile) == 1L, job_others < 0.05)
```

The three profiles differ in media use and in work. At prompts in profile
`r media_profile`, students used social media with probability
`r answer(media_profile, "on_social_media")`, watched TV or played video games
with probability `r answer(media_profile, "tv_video_games")`, and listened to
music with probability `r answer(media_profile, "listened_music")`. In profile
`r low_profile` the same probabilities are
`r answer(low_profile, "on_social_media")`,
`r answer(low_profile, "tv_video_games")` and
`r answer(low_profile, "listened_music")`, and time with friends
(`r answer(low_profile, "time_with_friends")` against
`r answer(media_profile, "time_with_friends")`) and walking
(`r answer(low_profile, "walking")` against `r answer(media_profile, "walking")`)
are somewhat more likely. Both report sports at about 0.07. At prompts in
profile `r job_profile` students worked at a part-time job with probability
`r answer(job_profile, "part_time_job")` and reported every other activity
with probability below 0.05. Profile `r media_profile` is therefore a
media-heavy pattern, profile `r low_profile` a pattern of little media use
with the remaining activities at their usual low rates, and profile
`r job_profile` a pattern of work with little else.

The response plot draws the same probabilities, one line per profile across
the items.

```{r responses-plot}
plot_responses(lca)
```

The media-heavy and low-media lines separate on the three media items and
nearly coincide on sports, while the work profile stands apart on the
part-time job item.

## Two student classes

The `"counts"` table gives the size of each profile and class, and the
`"profile_probabilities"` table the profile mix of each student class.

```{r mix}
get_results(lca, "counts")
get_results(lca, "profile_probabilities")
```

```{r class-values, include = FALSE}
counts <- subset(get_results(lca, "counts"), level == "individuals")
size <- function(k) {
  with(subset(counts, class == k), sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * effective_proportion))
}
mix <- get_results(lca, "profile_probabilities")
media_class <- with(subset(mix, profile == media_profile & probability > 0.5),
                    group_class)
other_class <- with(mix, setdiff(unique(group_class), media_class))
share <- function(g, k) {
  with(subset(mix, group_class == g & profile == k), sprintf("%.3f", probability))
}
class_size <- function(g) {
  with(subset(mix, group_class == g & profile == media_profile),
       sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * group_class_probability))
}
work_share <- function(g) {
  with(subset(mix, group_class == g & profile == job_profile), probability)
}
work_ratio <- work_share(other_class) / work_share(media_class)
# The text below describes the classes by these patterns; stop if they change.
stopifnot(length(media_class) == 1L, length(other_class) == 1L, work_ratio > 3)
```

The low-media profile holds `r size(low_profile)` of prompts, the media-heavy
profile `r size(media_profile)` and the work profile `r size(job_profile)`.
The student classes differ sharply in their mix. In class `r other_class`,
which holds `r class_size(other_class)` of students,
`r share(other_class, low_profile)` of prompts fall in the low-media profile,
`r share(other_class, job_profile)` in the work profile and only
`r share(other_class, media_profile)` in the media-heavy one. In class
`r media_class`, with `r class_size(media_class)` of students, the media-heavy
profile is the more common, at `r share(media_class, media_profile)`, and the
work profile almost absent, at `r share(media_class, job_profile)`.
Media-heavy leisure is therefore concentrated in a minority of students, and
for them it is the usual pattern, while most students almost never report it.
Part-time work appears mainly among the students of the low-media class.

The probability plot compares the two mixes.

```{r probabilities-plot}
plot_prevalence(lca)
```

Class `r other_class` runs close to one on the low-media profile and close to
zero on the media-heavy one; class `r media_class` divides its prompts between
those two profiles, with the larger share on the media-heavy profile.

## Classification certainty

Profiles and classes are estimated as posterior probabilities. Relative
entropy summarizes how concentrated those probabilities are, from 0
for no separation to 1 for certain assignment, and the `"classification"`
table reports the average posterior probability of each assigned class.

```{r classification}
get_results(lca, "entropy")
get_results(lca, "classification")
```

```{r classification-values, include = FALSE}
entropy <- get_results(lca, "entropy")
relative <- function(at) {
  with(subset(entropy, level == at), sprintf("%.3f", relative_entropy))
}
assigned <- get_results(lca, "classification")
posterior <- function(at, k) {
  with(subset(assigned, level == at & class == k), sprintf("%.3f", average_posterior))
}
```

Relative entropy is `r relative("individuals")` for prompts and
`r relative("groups")` for students. A single prompt answers eight yes/no
questions, which leaves its profile less certain; a student contributes many
prompts, which pins down the class. The average posterior probability is
`r posterior("individuals", job_profile)` for prompts assigned to the work
profile, `r posterior("individuals", low_profile)` for the low-media profile
and `r posterior("individuals", media_profile)` for the media-heavy one, and
`r posterior("groups", other_class)` and `r posterior("groups", media_class)`
for the two student classes. Conclusions about students are therefore well
supported, while an analysis of individual prompts should carry the posterior
probabilities forward.

## Local independence

The model assumes the items are independent within a profile. The
`"residuals"` table measures the association that each pair of items keeps
within a profile, with a chi-square test for each pair; the ten largest are
shown.

```{r residuals}
get_results(lca, "residuals") |> head(10)
```

```{r residual-values, include = FALSE}
residuals <- get_results(lca, "residuals")
largest <- head(residuals, 1)
walking <- subset(residuals, profile == sprintf("profile_%d", media_profile) &
                    indicator_2 == "walking") |> head(3)
# The text below names these pairs; stop if the results ever change.
stopifnot(with(largest, profile) == sprintf("profile_%d", job_profile),
          with(largest, indicator_1) == "on_social_media",
          with(largest, indicator_2) == "walking",
          identical(with(walking, indicator_1),
                    c("sports", "time_with_friends", "listened_music")))
pair <- function(rows, item) {
  with(subset(rows, indicator_1 == item), sprintf("%.3f", residual))
}
```

The largest residual, `r pair(largest, "on_social_media")`, links social media
and walking in the work profile, which holds about
`r with(largest, round(effective_n))` prompts, so it rests on few
observations. Next, in the media-heavy profile, come sports and walking
(`r pair(walking, "sports")`), friends and walking
(`r pair(walking, "time_with_friends")`) and music and walking
(`r pair(walking, "listened_music")`). Physical and social activities occur
together more often than three profiles allow, which is one reason BIC rewards
larger models: extra profiles can absorb this association.

## Uncertainty in the response probabilities

`parameter_inference()` gives standard errors and 95% Wald intervals for every
parameter. Several response probabilities lie on their bound: the work profile
reports TV or games, music and sports with probability zero and a part-time
job with probability one, and the low-media profile reports a part-time job
with probability zero. Wald inference does not apply at a bound, so
`boundary = "fix"` holds these probabilities at their values, leaves them out
of the table and reports the other parameters conditionally on them. The
intervals of the "yes" probabilities, in the rows whose `term` ends in `:yes`,
show how firmly the profiles are distinguished.

```{r inference}
parameter_inference(lca, boundary = "fix")
```

```{r inference-values, include = FALSE}
inference <- parameter_inference(lca, boundary = "fix")
interval <- function(k, item) {
  with(subset(inference, outcome == sprintf("profile_%d", k) &
                term == paste0(item, ":yes")),
       sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", conf_low, conf_high))
}
sports <- subset(inference, term == "sports:yes")
# The text below says the sports intervals overlap; stop if they ever do not.
stopifnot(nrow(sports) == 2L,
          with(sports, max(conf_low) < min(conf_high)))
```

The profiles are clearly separated on the media items: the interval for social
media is `r interval(media_profile, "on_social_media")` in the media-heavy
profile and `r interval(low_profile, "on_social_media")` in the low-media
profile. On sports the two intervals overlap almost entirely. The part-time
job probability in the media-heavy profile has an interval of
`r interval(media_profile, "part_time_job")`, close to zero, because very few
of its prompts report a job.

## Adding affect

A mixed model adds three affect ratings (happy, relaxed, exhausted, each from
1 to 7) as continuous indicators. `worried` is left out because about half of
its ratings are 1, which can push a profile's variance to its lower bound. The
same happens to `exhausted` with three profiles: one profile collects the
prompts rated 1 and its variance reaches the bound, so the mixed model is
fitted with two profiles and two classes.

```{r mixed}
mixed <- multilpa(student_esm,
                  vars = c("happy", "relaxed", "exhausted", activities),
                  categorical = activities, id = "student", n_profiles = 2,
                  n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
get_results(mixed)
get_results(mixed, "responses")
get_results(mixed, "profile_probabilities")
```

With affect included, the profiles become profiles of mood. Profile 1 has mean
ratings of 5.85 for happy, 5.59 for relaxed and 2.55 for exhausted; profile 2
has 3.59, 3.33 and 4.33. The activities now differ less and in a different
way: time with friends is reported at 0.188 of profile-1 prompts and 0.084 of
profile-2 prompts, social media at 0.269 and 0.315. Good mood goes with social
time more than with media use. The student classes remain distinct: 0.874 of
the prompts of class 1 fall in the low-mood profile, and 0.833 of those of
class 2 in the good-mood profile. The profiles a model finds are set by the
indicators it is given, so the choice of indicators is part of the question.

## Interpretation

Students' leisure at non-study prompts falls into three patterns: one defined
by social media, TV and music, one with little media use, and a small one of
part-time work with little else. The distinction that matters most is between
students: a majority almost never reports the media-heavy pattern, and a
minority reports it at more than half of their prompts. Part-time work appears
mainly among the majority. That student-level result is well supported by the
classification diagnostics, while the assignment of any single prompt is less
certain.

## Limitations

The data contain only prompts at which the student had not studied, so the
patterns describe leisure time, not the whole day. The three-profile model
leaves association between physical and social activities within its
profiles, and larger models fit better by BIC but are not stable across starts
on these data. The choice of three profiles itself depends on enough starts:
with few, the model stops at a lower maximum and two profiles are chosen. Prompts are treated as independent given the student's class, so the
model ignores the order of prompts within a day. The associations are
observational and say nothing about causes.

## Reference

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on
multiple time scales. *Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft, 27*(1),
147-168. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8>
